extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and lawyers dealing with preliminary injunctions in patent cases
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and defenses governing motions for preliminary injunctions in patent litigation, including what facts and proofs will sustain or defeat such motions, when bonds may substitute for injunctions, and when injunctions may be dissolved or reinstated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences by way of traverse vs confession and avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The defences which a defendant may make to a motion for a preliminary injunction may be by way of traverse, or by way of confession and avoidance. A defence of the former sort consists in denying, and attempting to disprove, one or more of the facts which constitute the complainant's prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A denial alone is useless, even when embodied in an answer. Where the denial is supported by affidavits which contradict those of the complainant, the judge will refuse the injunction if he believes the defendant's affidavits to be the true ones, or if he is unable to decide which set of deponents tell the truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction is summary and dangerous; effect of defendant's evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: No remedy invoked in patent cases is so summary in operation, or so dangerous to justice as a preliminary injunction, and the courts will not apply that remedy to cases where the complainant's prima facie evidence of a right thereto is overthrown or seriously damaged by the evidence of the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant's evidence substantially damages or overthrows plaintiff's prima facie case, courts will refuse an injunction; judges require weightier proof for this summary remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confession and avoidance may aver prior adjudication or interpose outside facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Defences by way of confession and avoidance to motions for preliminary injunctions may confess and avoid the adjudication or acquiescence upon which the plaintiff bases the presumption of the validity of his patent; or may interpose any one of several facts entirely outside of the complainant's prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confession-and-avoidance pleadings can negate the presumptive effect of prior judgments or rely on collateral facts (e.g., prior use, license, expiration). They must be supported by evidence where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior adjudication can be averted only by strong showing
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of an adjudication may be averted by evidence of some good defence to the patent, together with evidence showing that defence not to have been interposed in the prior adjudicated case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower courts sometimes require that such a new defence be established beyond a reasonable doubt. A new defence that cannot withstand the application of what was decided in the adjudicated case must fail to avert a preliminary injunction. Examples of acceptable showings include inconsistency with a former decision, a rehearing pending, a jury verdict still subject to new-trial motion, an appeal to a higher court, or a prior use not pleaded in the earlier case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome effect of prior adjudication (exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of a prior adjudication may sometimes be averted by showing that it is inconsistent with a former decision of the court, or that the adjudged case has been taken under advisement for rehearing, or that the adjudged case has gone no further than a jury verdict pending a new trial, or that it has been taken to a higher court for review, or that a prior use not pleaded in the prior adjudication would have caused a contrary decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are specific factual situations in which an earlier adjudication need not preclude a preliminary injunction; courts examine procedural posture and completeness of prior adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence may be a foundation for injunction but can be averted
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of acquiescence, as a foundation for a preliminary injunction, may be averted by evidence that it was not general, or was not genuine: by proof that while some acquiesced in the patent, many others did not; or by proof that those who did acquiesce did so collusively and not because they believed the patent to be invulnerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also, the effect of acquiescence may be averted by evidence or arguments which clearly show that the patent is really invalid. Courts scrutinize the breadth and sincerity of alleged acquiescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent expiration, repeal or foreign expiration as defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that the patent sued upon has been repealed, or that it has expired by its own limitation, or because of the expiration of some foreign patent for the same invention, is of course a good defence to a motion for a preliminary injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent that has expired before decision defeats a PI even if it had not expired when the motion was made. Whether imminent expiration favors or disfavors an injunction depends on circumstances; it may be a reason either for granting or refusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: License is a good defence; proof standards and construction of documents
rubrics_metrics.description: A license is a good defence to a motion for a preliminary injunction; but where a license is disputed, it must be established by a preponderance of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When license questions depend upon construction of documents, the court will construe them on a motion for a preliminary injunction unless it appears evidence is proper and necessary to determine parties' intention. Forfeiture for non-payment of royalty may permit PI unless royalty is paid within a reasonable time; forfeiture by forbidden use may permit injunction as to that use but not authorized uses. A PI will not be used to enforce forfeiture where the wrongdoing can be compensated, and PI may be refused if forfeiture was necessitated by complainant's bad faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel as a defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel is also a good defence to a motion for a preliminary injunction, and will prevail against a motion for that relief upon the same facts that would make it prevail in an action at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply ordinary estoppel principles in the interlocutory injunction context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches and delay bar preliminary injunctions unless excused
rubrics_metrics.description: Laches is a good defence to a motion for a preliminary injunction; and delay works laches, unless it is excused by some fact which renders it reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant delay is that occurring after the infringement sued upon was committed, not delay before it. Courts have found various delays (three months, one year, eighteen months, two years, three years, five years, six years) either excused or fatal depending on circumstances like smallness of infringement, excuse for complainant's occupation, notification attempts, pendency of test cases, and whether defendant was misled. Delay after suit but before making the PI motion (e.g., two months unexcused) may be fatal if it seriously misleads defendant or continues until defendant closes interlocutory evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prima facie case: generally bound to grant injunction if not overthrown
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the complainant has made out a prima facie case for a preliminary injunction, and where the defendant has not overthrown that case, the court is generally bound to grant such an injunction, upon all or upon pari of the claims of the patent, according to the merits of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The effect on non-parties usually cannot be considered on such a motion. Courts balance the harsh and arbitrary character of a PI against the difficulty of recovering damages or profits and the lack of adequate remedy pendente lite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferred or graduated operation of injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary injunctions are not always made immediately operative; an injunction may sometimes be made to take effect a few days or even a few months in the future, and sometimes at graduated future intervals upon distinct parts of the defendant's doings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may delay operation to accommodate equitable reasons or phase in relief across different activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option to give bond instead of submitting to injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Under some circumstances, the court can give the defendant the option to submit to an injunction or to give a bond to secure any decree for profits or damages which may ultimately be awarded against him; but a bond can be required only in a case where an injunction must issue if the bond is not given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The option should be granted only in proper circumstances; where it is not warranted, it cannot be demanded by defendant nor should court grant it. If defendant chooses bonds but cannot promptly furnish them, an injunction may issue with order dissolving upon filing proper bonds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances warranting bond option (enumerated factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant may sometimes be entitled to the option of giving bonds instead of being enjoined where: complainant habitually licenses rather than manufactures; infringing machinery contains costly parts not covered by patent; infringing article purchased in good faith under junior patent; constructed by defendant himself; defendant is only a seller or only a user; a suit against the manufacturer is pending; prior adjudication is appealed and pending; new evidence is to be taken for interlocutory hearing; patent will soon expire; injunction would be very damaging to defendant and not particularly beneficial to complainant; public policy forbids discontinuance; complainant does not employ the invention; or injunction would operate unjustly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These circumstances are illustrative and courts examine the totality of circumstances. The option is not automatic; absence of special reasons precludes granting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of bond amount
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure of the amount of the bond is the approximate amount of profits which the defendant will make from the time when the order is made to the termination of the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bond should approximate anticipated profits during interlocutory period so as to secure any eventual decree for profits or damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on using PI to enforce forfeiture or force compromises/contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no part of the legitimate office of a preliminary injunction to force the defendant to compromise a disputed claim, nor to compel him to give the complainant a contract to purchase specimens of the patented thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PI should not be employed to coerce settlement or commercial arrangements beyond equitable relief; injunctions enforce rights, not force bargains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may require security from plaintiff (Clayton Act / historical practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formerly it was in the discretion of the court whether a bond should be required of the plaintiff as a condition to the issuance of a preliminary injunction. By Section 18 of the Clayton Act it was provided that no restraining order or interlocutory order of injunction shall issue except upon the giving of security by the applicant in such sum as the court or judge may deem proper, conditioned upon payment of such costs or damages as may be incurred by any party wrongfully enjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs may be required to give security to protect defendants from wrongful injunctions; historically courts conditioned bonds on plaintiff's ultimate success, particularly where injunction would seriously injure defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction not displaced solely by adequacy of legal remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary injunction cannot be averted on the sole ground that an action at law for the damages to be caused by the infringement would be a plain, adequate and complete remedy therefor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts cannot determine on affidavits whether damages would be adequate in a particular case; even where damages appear adequate, complainant retains choice of equitable relief analogously to specific performance; motions for PI should not be defeated merely on the possibility of damages recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent decrees vs judicial decisions when defendant withdraws opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant withdraws his opposition to a motion for a preliminary injunction before the motion is decided, the injunction may be granted by consent; but the court will decline to render a decision. A consent decree will be entered as a consent decree, and not as one based on a conclusion of the judicial mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule prevents parties from obtaining binding judicial rulings where there is no real contest, protecting strangers to the litigation from collusive outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to dissolve injunction: timing and grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to dissolve a preliminary injunction may be made at any time, upon reasonable notice to the complainant's solicitor; and it will be promptly granted where the judge becomes convinced that the granting of the injunction was erroneous in point of law, or where the defendant positively proves any fact which would have been fatal to the motion for the preliminary injunction if presented at the time that motion was heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissolution may also be based on facts arising after the injunction (e.g., assignment of interest, failure to prosecute with required speed, false advertising for effect, reversal on appeal). Courts act promptly once convinced of error or new fatal facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for legal-error motions to dissolve
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to dissolve an injunction for error in point of law must be based on a point which was established after the injunction was granted, or which was obviously overlooked or misweighed by the judge at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is unprofessional and generally unavailing to seek dissolution by rearguing old, well-understood points; courts expect new legal developments or clear oversight rather than mere disagreement with prior reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to dissolve for newly discovered facts: burden and evidence balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to dissolve an injunction on account of newly discovered facts requires the mover to assume the burden of establishing those facts; because when an injunction is once granted, it is presumed to have been granted rightfully until the contrary is made to appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits and evidence to disprove moving papers may be introduced by complainant; then defendant may present counter-evidence. The judge must balance the documents and ascertain where the weight lies, and will decide against the mover unless his papers preponderate. Service of affidavits before hearing is called for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to reinstate dissolved injunction: timing and standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to reinstate a dissolved injunction may be made at any time; but it will not be granted on the same state of the case as that which existed when the injunction was dissolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reinstated preliminary injunction may be again dissolved on any new state of facts showing its continuation would be unjust. In patent cases, repeated cycles of issuing and dissolving are rare after the first dissolution unless great clearness and pressing necessity are shown.
